cards.statement: Managed nodes require an installed Ansible agent before the control node runs tasks.
cards.explanation: Managed nodes normally need no Ansible installation; the control node manages them over a connection.
cards.misconception: Managed hosts need a resident Ansible agent.

cards.statement: Running most Ansible modules on Linux managed nodes requires Python on those managed nodes.
cards.explanation: Most Linux modules use Python on the managed node. A connection alone does not meet their runtime requirements.

cards.statement: Ansible uses the ssh connection plugin by default to reach Linux managed nodes.
cards.explanation: Ansible selects the ssh plugin as its default connection transport for managed hosts.

cards.statement: Ansible executes copied Python module code on the control node during a remote task.
cards.explanation: For a remote task, Ansible sends Python module code to the managed node, which executes it and returns the result.
cards.misconception: The control node executes the Python module code for remote tasks.

cards.statement: Setting `ansible_python_interpreter` to a path makes Ansible discover a replacement when that path fails.
cards.explanation: An explicit interpreter path disables discovery. Ansible uses the specified interpreter.
cards.misconception: An explicit interpreter path is a preferred discovery candidate.

cards.statement: With `ansible-pull`, each managed node checks out playbooks from Git and runs them on itself.
cards.explanation: Pull mode reverses Ansible's default push model: a crontab on the node runs ansible-pull, which fetches the configuration and manages that machine locally.

cards.statement: The `ansible` command uses ansible.builtin.shell for ad hoc tasks by default.
cards.explanation: The ansible command defaults to ansible.builtin.command. Use -m to select a different module.
cards.misconception: Ad hoc commands use the shell module by default.

cards.statement: In an ad hoc command, `-u deploy` selects deploy as the privilege escalation user.
cards.explanation: The -u option chooses the user Ansible uses to connect to the managed host.
cards.misconception: The remote connection user is the privilege escalation target.

cards.statement: The host pattern `web:db` selects hosts belonging to either the web group or the db group.
cards.explanation: A colon combines groups as a union; hosts from either named group match.

cards.statement: Using `ansible web --limit db` can add hosts outside web to the ad hoc task's targets.
cards.explanation: --limit further restricts the original host pattern. This command targets hosts in both groups.
cards.misconception: A limit widens the host pattern by adding its own matches.

cards.statement: Ansible reads `~/.ansible/hosts` as its inventory source with the default configuration.
cards.explanation: Ansible's default inventory source is /etc/ansible/hosts.
cards.misconception: The default inventory lives in the control user's home directory.

cards.statement: Ansible runs a task once per host when that host matches several targeted inventory groups.
cards.explanation: Membership in several matching groups still identifies one host for task execution.

cards.statement: Ansible uses `ansible_host` as the connection address for an inventory alias.
cards.explanation: Set ansible_host to the destination hostname or IP address when inventory uses an alias.

cards.statement: ansible-playbook reads `group_vars` beside the playbook as a source of inventory group variables.
cards.explanation: ansible-playbook also loads group variable files from beside the playbook.

cards.statement: Ansible resolves a shared variable to the parent group's value over the child group's value.
cards.explanation: A child group's variable overrides the same variable from its parent group.
cards.misconception: Parent group variables override values from child groups.

cards.statement: Ansible merges same-level inventory groups alphabetically when their priorities match.
cards.explanation: For conflicting variables, the later alphabetical group wins among equal-priority groups at that level.

cards.statement: Ansible uses `ansible_group_priority` from `group_vars` to order same-level merges.
cards.explanation: Set ansible_group_priority in inventory; Ansible needs it before loading group_vars.
cards.misconception: Group variable files can set their own group's merge priority.

cards.statement: With `-i first.yml -i second.yml`, a variable set for one group in both files takes the `first.yml` value.
cards.explanation: When two -i sources set the same group's variable, the source given later on the command line wins, so the value here comes from second.yml.
cards.misconception: The first inventory source takes priority over later sources.

cards.statement: Setting `enable_plugins` appends inventory plugins to Ansible's default enabled list.
cards.explanation: enable_plugins replaces the default list, so include the plugins you want to retain.
cards.misconception: Explicit plugin enablement adds entries to the default list.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.constructed` discovers new hosts before applying its `keyed_groups` rules.
cards.explanation: The constructed plugin groups existing hosts and derives variables from earlier inventory sources.
cards.misconception: The constructed plugin discovers additional hosts.

cards.statement: The Ansible docs recommend inventory plugins over scripts for dynamic inventory.
cards.explanation: The guide favors plugins because they benefit from recent ansible-core updates.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.command` can interpret a pipe as a shell pipeline on the managed host.
cards.explanation: command passes arguments to the program rather than a shell. Use ansible.builtin.shell for pipelines.
cards.misconception: The command module processes shell operators.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.command` expands environment variables in arguments through Python by default.
cards.explanation: command uses Python to expand environment-variable arguments before invoking the program.

cards.statement: `creates: /tmp/ready` makes `ansible.builtin.command` run when `/tmp/ready` already exists.
cards.explanation: command skips its command when the path given to creates already exists.
cards.misconception: creates triggers execution when its path exists.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.raw` sends its command through the connection, bypassing the module subsystem.
cards.explanation: raw sends a command directly through the connection rather than packaging a normal module invocation.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.package` converts the name `libyaml-dev` to `libyaml-devel` when it runs on a Red Hat host.
cards.explanation: package delegates to the host's package manager module; the playbook supplies distribution-appropriate names.
cards.misconception: The generic package module translates distribution-specific package names.

cards.statement: With `--check`, Ansible executes modules normally when their `check_mode` support is documented as `none`.
cards.explanation: Check mode skips modules that lack support, leaving their requested changes unapplied.
cards.misconception: Check mode falls back to normal execution for unsupported modules.

cards.statement: With `--check`, `ansible.builtin.command` uses `creates` to predict changes from file existence.
cards.explanation: command checks the creates path and predicts its changed status in check mode while leaving the command unexecuted.

cards.statement: During a playbook run using `--check`, `check_mode: false` makes Ansible skip the task carrying that keyword.
cards.explanation: check_mode: false forces normal task execution even during a --check playbook run.
cards.misconception: Disabling check mode skips the task during a simulated run.

cards.statement: Check mode can miss predictions for tasks conditioned on earlier registered results.
cards.explanation: Simulation can omit results needed by later conditions, leaving dependent tasks with no useful prediction.

cards.statement: With `--diff` alone, `ansible.builtin.copy` applies requested file changes while reporting differences.
cards.explanation: Diff mode reports changes during normal execution; adding --check instead reports proposed changes.

cards.statement: A task with `diff: false` returns before-and-after file content when the playbook uses `--diff`.
cards.explanation: diff: false suppresses that task's diff even when the playbook uses --diff.
cards.misconception: The command-line option overrides a task's diff suppression.

cards.statement: When a play and one of its tasks both set `remote_user`, Ansible uses the play's value for that task.
cards.explanation: A task's remote_user overrides the play's value; the more specific keyword wins.
cards.misconception: Play-level keywords override values set on tasks.

source.title: Controlling how Ansible behaves: precedence rules

cards.statement: `ansible-playbook --step` prompts the operator before Ansible executes each task.
cards.explanation: --step runs a playbook interactively, letting the operator confirm tasks as execution proceeds.

cards.statement: Ansible queues a notified handler when its notifying task reports `ok`.
cards.explanation: Ansible queues a handler from a task's notify list when that task reports changed.
cards.misconception: An ok result triggers handler notifications.

cards.statement: Ansible runs a handler once per flush even when several tasks notify it.
cards.explanation: Ansible coalesces repeated notifications for a handler within a flush, avoiding repeated execution.

cards.statement: Ansible runs queued handlers in the order that each task first notifies them.
cards.explanation: Ansible executes queued handlers in definition order, regardless of notification order.
cards.misconception: Handler execution follows notification order.

cards.statement: A changed task can notify several handlers by naming their shared `listen` topic.
cards.explanation: A notification to a listen topic selects the handlers listening to that topic, independently of their names.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.meta: flush_handlers` runs the handlers that tasks have already notified.
cards.explanation: flush_handlers triggers pending handler notifications at that point in the play.

cards.statement: A role can keep its handlers in a scope separate from the play's other handlers.
cards.explanation: Ansible inserts role handlers into the play's shared handler scope, making them available outside the role.
cards.misconception: Roles isolate handler names from the rest of the play.

cards.statement: Ansible filters notified handlers with `--tags` in the same way it filters ordinary tasks.
cards.explanation: Handlers ignore tags; their assigned tags do not filter handler execution.
cards.misconception: Handler tags control execution like ordinary task tags.

cards.statement: With `force_handlers: true`, Ansible runs notified handlers on hosts with later task failures.
cards.explanation: force_handlers preserves pending handlers after a task failure; an unreachable host can still prevent execution.

cards.statement: A leading underscore gives an Ansible variable private visibility.
cards.explanation: Ansible applies normal variable scope to names beginning with an underscore; the prefix adds no privacy.
cards.misconception: Underscore-prefixed variables receive private visibility.

cards.statement: `ansible-playbook site.yml -e @release.yml` loads extra vars from the YAML file `release.yml`.
cards.explanation: Prefix a variable file's name with `@` when supplying its contents through `-e`.

cards.statement: Ansible chooses the extra-vars value when the same variable exists in other variable sources.
cards.explanation: Extra vars occupy the top of Ansible's variable precedence order, so competing definitions yield to them.

source.title: Controlling how Ansible behaves: precedence rules

cards.statement: Ansible uses an inventory value over a matching variable defined in a role's defaults.
cards.explanation: Role defaults provide starting values at the lowest variable precedence; inventory values override them.

cards.statement: After `ansible.builtin.set_fact` sets `release: new`, later tasks read the play `vars` value `release: old`.
cards.explanation: A regular `ansible.builtin.set_fact` host variable outranks play `vars`, so later tasks read `new`.
cards.misconception: Play variables keep priority over variables set during execution.

cards.statement: With play-level `remote_user: deploy`, adding `-u ops` makes Ansible connect as `ops`.
cards.explanation: The play's `remote_user` keyword overrides the command-line `-u` setting, so Ansible connects as `deploy`.
cards.misconception: Command-line connection options override playbook keywords.

source.title: Controlling how Ansible behaves: precedence rules

cards.statement: A host's registered variable remains available in subsequent plays of the same playbook run.
cards.explanation: Ansible keeps registered task results as host variables in memory for the current playbook run.

cards.statement: Ansible leaves the registered name undefined when a task's `when` evaluates to false.
cards.explanation: A task skipped by `when` still creates its registered variable containing the skipped result.
cards.misconception: A conditional skip prevents creation of a registered variable.

cards.statement: With `cacheable: true`, `ansible.builtin.set_fact` creates a host variable and a lower-priority fact copy.
cards.explanation: The two copies coexist in the current run; the fact copy is eligible for persistence through a configured fact cache.

cards.statement: Ansible combines keys from repeated dictionary variable definitions as it resolves precedence.
cards.explanation: The default `replace` behavior selects the winning dictionary as a whole, replacing earlier definitions.
cards.misconception: Ansible automatically merges dictionary keys across variable sources.

cards.statement: With `remote_user: deploy` and `ansible_user: ops`, Ansible connects as `ops`.
cards.explanation: The connection variable `ansible_user` overrides the equivalent playbook keyword `remote_user`.

source.title: Controlling how Ansible behaves: precedence rules

cards.statement: Ansible merges values from discovered `ansible.cfg` files while searching for its configuration.
cards.explanation: Ansible uses the first configuration file found in its search order and ignores the remaining files.
cards.misconception: Ansible combines settings from multiple configuration files.

cards.statement: Ansible automatically runs `ansible.builtin.setup` at the start of a play to gather facts.
cards.explanation: The initial gathering step collects managed-host information for use by the play's tasks.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: With gathering set to `smart`, Ansible reuses a host's facts in later plays of the same run.
cards.explanation: After discovering a host's facts, smart gathering avoids gathering them again as subsequent plays address that host.

cards.statement: Ansible keeps the `ansible_` prefix on system fact keys inside `ansible_facts`.
cards.explanation: Read the OS family as `ansible_facts['os_family']`; system fact keys drop the `ansible_` prefix inside this dictionary.
cards.misconception: Fact dictionary keys retain the prefix shown in setup module output.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.20, Ansible deprecates reading injected top-level fact variables.
cards.explanation: Accessing injected fact variables emits a deprecation warning; read facts through the `ansible_facts` dictionary.
cards.volatilityNote: The default for fact injection is scheduled to change in ansible-core 2.24.

cards.statement: Ansible limits fact collection to matching names when `ansible.builtin.setup` uses `filter`.
cards.explanation: The `filter` option limits returned facts; `gather_subset` controls which groups of facts the module collects.
cards.misconception: The setup filter limits collection rather than the returned data.

cards.statement: Ansible exposes a facts.d file's custom data through `ansible_facts['local']`.
cards.explanation: The local namespace keeps custom facts from `.fact` files separate from built-in system facts.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: Ansible refreshes `inventory_hostname` to match `ansible_facts['hostname']` during fact gathering.
cards.explanation: The `inventory_hostname` value comes from inventory, so gathering facts leaves that identifier intact.
cards.misconception: Fact gathering updates the inventory identifier to the system hostname.

cards.statement: After adding a `.fact` file, Ansible needs another `ansible.builtin.setup` call to use it in the same play.
cards.explanation: Re-run `ansible.builtin.setup` after installing the custom fact so later tasks in that play can read it.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: Ansible's default memory fact cache supplies gathered facts to the next playbook run.
cards.explanation: The memory cache retains facts for the current Ansible execution; its contents end with that run.
cards.misconception: The default fact cache persists data across playbook executions.

cards.statement: Ansible automatically gathers another host's `ansible_facts` when a task reads them through `hostvars`.
cards.explanation: Access another host's facts through `hostvars` after those facts have been gathered or loaded from a fact cache.
cards.misconception: Looking up a host's facts causes Ansible to collect them on demand.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: Ansible removes failed hosts from `ansible_play_hosts` as they leave the active play.
cards.explanation: The `ansible_play_hosts` list tracks hosts still active in the play and excludes failed or unreachable hosts.

cards.statement: Ansible renders task templates on the control node before sending the task to a managed host.
cards.explanation: The controller resolves template expressions locally and sends the values needed for the task to its target.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.copy` can render Jinja2 expressions inside a source file before transferring that file.
cards.explanation: Use ansible.builtin.template when file contents need Jinja2 rendering. The copy module transfers the source file's existing content.
cards.misconception: The copy module evaluates Jinja2 expressions embedded in source files.

cards.statement: Ansible requires quotes around an inline YAML value starting with a Jinja2 expression such as `{{ name }}`.
cards.explanation: YAML treats an opening `{` as mapping syntax. Quote the entire value so Ansible receives the intended template string.

cards.statement: Ansible substitutes an empty string when a task template reads an undefined variable.
cards.explanation: An undefined variable used in a task's template raises an error rather than becoming an empty string.
cards.misconception: Ansible silently fills missing template variables with empty strings.

cards.statement: Using `default(omit)` lets Ansible omit a module option whose input variable is undefined.
cards.explanation: When an expression resolves to omit, Ansible removes that option from the arguments passed to the module.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, `ansible.builtin.bool` reports a hard error for unrecognized input.
cards.explanation: Unrecognized input produces a deprecation warning while the bool filter still returns a boolean value.
cards.misconception: Unrecognized bool-filter input immediately fails conversion.
cards.volatilityNote: Unrecognized-input coercion is deprecated; the warning is planned to become an error in ansible-core 2.23.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.dict2items` produces two-element lists containing dictionary keys and values.
cards.explanation: The dict2items filter returns a list of dictionaries with `key` and `value` fields, pairing each source key with its value.
cards.misconception: The dict2items filter returns key-value pairs as lists rather than dictionaries.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.selectattr` turns matching objects into their selected attribute values.
cards.explanation: The selectattr filter tests the chosen attribute and returns the matching original objects.
cards.misconception: The selectattr filter projects attribute values instead of selecting whole objects.

cards.statement: Ansible's `query()` function returns lookup results as a list, ready for a task's loop.
cards.explanation: The query function is shorthand for `lookup(..., wantlist=True)`, which supplies list results.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, `{{ ['web1', 'web2'] | replace('web', 'db') }}` returns a string instead of a list.
cards.explanation: replace works on strings, so it turns the list into text, and 2.19 removed the final literal-evaluation pass that used to parse such text back into a list. Use map('replace', ...) to keep a list.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, Ansible returns `{{ range(0, 3) }}` as a list when templating a variable.
cards.explanation: The range function produces a range object. Convert it with `| list` before returning it from an Ansible template.
cards.misconception: Ansible automatically converts a range object into a list at template finalization.

cards.statement: Ansible reads `when: flag` as a raw Jinja2 expression using the variable `flag`.
cards.explanation: A when expression refers to variable names directly. Ansible evaluates the expression as the task's execution condition.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, Ansible accepts an arbitrary string result from `when` by default.
cards.explanation: A when condition must return a boolean by default. A string result produces an error instead of implicit truthy evaluation.
cards.misconception: Ansible treats nonempty string results as true conditions.

cards.statement: Ansible evaluates `result is failed` from the result's status, even when `result.stderr` is empty.
cards.explanation: The failed test checks the task result's failed status. Empty stderr does not make a failed result successful.

source.title: ansible.builtin.failed test – did the task fail

cards.statement: Ansible evaluates a looped task's `when` condition once before it starts processing the items.
cards.explanation: Ansible evaluates when separately for each loop item, so one task can run for some items and skip others.
cards.misconception: Ansible uses one condition result for the complete loop.

cards.statement: Ansible skips a task looping over `targets | default([])` when `targets` is undefined.
cards.explanation: default([]) supplies an empty list for an undefined variable, leaving no items for the task to process.

cards.statement: The loops guide marks `with_<lookup>` forms as deprecated in favor of `loop`.
cards.explanation: with_<lookup> forms remain supported. The loops guide explicitly says these forms are not deprecated.
cards.misconception: The loop keyword deprecates with_<lookup> syntax.

cards.statement: A `loop` over a nested list flattens one level just as `with_items` does.
cards.explanation: with_items flattens one level implicitly. A loop needs flatten(1) to reproduce that behavior.
cards.misconception: The loop keyword implicitly flattens nested items.

cards.statement: `loop_control.label` changes the value that Ansible passes to the looped task as `item`.
cards.explanation: loop_control.label changes the displayed label; the task still receives the original item.
cards.misconception: The loop label replaces item data.

cards.statement: Ansible reports a looped task as `skipped` only when every item is skipped.
cards.explanation: The loop's overall skipped status means the complete set of iterations was skipped, rather than just some items.

cards.statement: Ansible applies a block's `when` condition separately before each task in that block.
cards.explanation: Ansible reevaluates the inherited condition for each enclosed task.

cards.statement: A block can repeat its complete task list for each item supplied to the block's `loop`.
cards.explanation: Ansible rejects loop as a block directive.
cards.misconception: Blocks support a loop directive.

cards.statement: A rescue task can inspect the failed task's return data through `ansible_failed_result`.
cards.explanation: ansible_failed_result holds the triggering task's captured result for rescue tasks.

cards.statement: Ansible runs a block's `always` tasks after a task in `rescue` returns `failed`.
cards.explanation: A task failure in rescue still permits execution of the block's always section.

cards.statement: Ansible continues the play on a host after its `rescue` tasks successfully handle a block failure.
cards.explanation: Successful rescue clears the original task's failed status and keeps the host executing the play.

cards.statement: Ansible starts a block's `rescue` section when a task reports its host as unreachable.
cards.explanation: Ansible excludes unreachable hosts from a block's rescue processing.
cards.misconception: Unreachable hosts trigger rescue.

cards.statement: After a task fails outside a block, Ansible continues that host's subsequent play tasks.
cards.explanation: Ansible stops further play tasks on the failed host by default, while other hosts continue.
cards.misconception: Ansible continues ordinary tasks on a host after an unhandled failure.

cards.statement: With `ignore_errors: true`, Ansible keeps an unreachable host active for later tasks.
cards.explanation: ignore_errors handles task failures. Use ignore_unreachable to keep scheduling tasks for a host reported unreachable.
cards.misconception: ignore_errors also ignores unreachable-host status.

cards.statement: Ansible marks a task failed when any condition in a `failed_when` list is true.
cards.explanation: A failed_when list uses implicit and, so the task fails when its listed conditions are true together.
cards.misconception: Ansible joins failed_when list entries with logical or.

cards.statement: `changed_when: false` makes Ansible report an otherwise successful command task as `ok`.
cards.explanation: The changed_when override alters the reported change status while the successful command still executes.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.17, Ansible runs `rescue` on every host after a block fails with `any_errors_fatal`.
cards.explanation: any_errors_fatal spreads the block's failure across hosts, so rescue also runs on hosts where the task succeeded.

cards.statement: With `serial`, Ansible aborts the play when a batch's failure percentage equals `max_fail_percentage`.
cards.explanation: A serial batch's failure percentage must exceed max_fail_percentage to abort the play; matching the threshold is insufficient.
cards.misconception: Reaching max_fail_percentage is enough to abort a play.

cards.statement: Ansible requires each standard role subdirectory to exist before loading a role.
cards.explanation: A role includes the directories it uses; unused standard directories are optional.
cards.misconception: Missing standard subdirectories make a role invalid.

cards.statement: With a role `web` in both `roles/` beside the playbook and `roles_path`, Ansible loads the `roles_path` copy.
cards.explanation: The playbook's adjacent roles/ directory takes priority over roles_path.
cards.misconception: roles_path outranks the playbook-adjacent roles directory.

cards.statement: Ansible executes dependencies from `meta/main.yml` before the role that declares them.
cards.explanation: Declared dependencies run first, placing prerequisites ahead of the declaring role's tasks.

cards.statement: Ansible runs identical `roles:` entries separately by default.
cards.explanation: Ansible deduplicates matching roles entries within one play unless the role enables allow_duplicates.
cards.misconception: Identical roles entries each cause a separate execution.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.include_role` keeps role vars and defaults within the role's scope by default.
cards.explanation: include_role defaults public to false, so later play tasks do not gain that role's vars and defaults.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.15, Ansible confines vars passed under a `roles:` entry to that role's scope.
cards.explanation: Inline vars supplied to a roles entry stay local rather than becoming play variables.

cards.statement: By default, Ansible validates role arguments from `meta/argument_specs.yml` while parsing the playbook.
cards.explanation: Ansible validates role arguments at the beginning of role execution, before its normal tasks.
cards.misconception: Role argument validation happens while parsing the playbook, before execution starts.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.include_tasks` repeats the included task group for each item when the include uses `loop`.
cards.explanation: Ansible processes the include for each loop item, loading and executing the task file again for that iteration.

cards.statement: Ansible evaluates `when` on `ansible.builtin.import_tasks` once before the imported task group starts.
cards.explanation: An imported when condition belongs to each imported task and is evaluated again before each task executes.
cards.misconception: An import's when condition is evaluated once for the whole imported group.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.import_playbook` imports another playbook as a task inside a play's `tasks` list.
cards.explanation: import_playbook belongs at the playbook's top level, where it imports a list of plays.
cards.misconception: import_playbook belongs inside a play's task list.

cards.statement: Ansible uses a play's `collections` list to resolve unqualified filter names.
cards.explanation: The collections keyword sets the search order for modules and action plugins. A filter needs its FQCN to select content from a collection.
cards.misconception: The collections keyword also supplies the search path for filters.

cards.statement: A role automatically inherits the `collections` search list defined by its calling play.
cards.explanation: A play's collections list stays outside the role's search settings. Set the role's own collections list in its meta/main.yml.
cards.misconception: A play's collections search list flows into the roles it calls.

cards.statement: A role inside a collection automatically searches that collection first for a short module name.
cards.explanation: A role's containing collection leads its implicit search path, so tasks in the role can address that collection's modules by short name.

cards.statement: The Ansible docs recommend FQCNs over the `collections` keyword for references to collection content.
cards.explanation: The collections guide favors explicit module or plugin references over relying on a collections search list.

cards.statement: `ansible-galaxy collection install` places collections under `~/.ansible/collections` by default.
cards.explanation: The default collection destination belongs to the user running the installer; ansible-galaxy stores the collections beneath it.

cards.statement: `ansible-galaxy collection install` automatically replaces an installed collection with its newest version.
cards.explanation: Use --upgrade to request an installed collection's upgrade. An ordinary install retains a collection that already satisfies the requested version.
cards.misconception: A normal collection install refreshes an already installed collection to the newest available version.

cards.statement: `ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml` supports installing roles and collections from the same file.
cards.explanation: A requirements file can contain both roles and collections sections for one install invocation.

source.title: Installing roles and collections from the same requirements.yml file

cards.statement: A role's `requirements.yml` version entry supports ranges such as `>=1.0.0,<2.0.0`.
cards.explanation: Role requirements select a specific version. Comparison ranges apply to collection requirements.
cards.misconception: Role requirements accept the version-range syntax used by collection requirements.

cards.statement: `ansible-galaxy` uses supplied signatures to verify a collection installed from a local `tar.gz` file.
cards.explanation: Galaxy signature verification applies to collections obtained from distribution servers. Local tarball installs bypass user-provided signatures.
cards.misconception: User-provided signatures are checked for a local collection tarball installation.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.21, ansible-galaxy installs collections with incompatible `requires_ansible` for later validation.
cards.explanation: Galaxy excludes incompatible collection versions from installation by default, checking requires_ansible against the running ansible-core.
cards.misconception: Galaxy installs collections despite incompatible requires_ansible metadata and postpones the compatibility check.

cards.statement: The `ansible` community package bundles a curated collection set alongside the ansible-core runtime.
cards.explanation: Installing ansible supplies community-selected collections in addition to the core runtime and its builtin content.

cards.statement: Ansible Vault accepts standard input as the plaintext source for `ansible-vault encrypt_string`.
cards.explanation: Pipe the plaintext into encrypt_string; --stdin-name assigns the variable name for that input.

cards.statement: `ansible-vault rekey` rotates the password for a single encrypted value embedded in a plaintext YAML file.
cards.explanation: Individually encrypted variables need newly encrypted values for password rotation; rekey handles whole encrypted files.
cards.misconception: Rekey handles individually encrypted variables as well as whole encrypted files.

cards.statement: Ansible reads task definitions from a whole-file encrypted YAML task file when given its Vault password.
cards.explanation: Task definitions remain usable by Ansible when their source file has file-level Vault encryption.

cards.statement: `ansible-vault encrypt` accepts a binary file as input alongside Ansible's structured data files.
cards.explanation: File-level Vault encryption works on arbitrary file contents, including binary data.

cards.statement: With `--vault-id prod@./vault-pass`, Ansible passes the `prod` label as an argument to that executable script.
cards.explanation: Ansible passes the label to password client scripts named with a -client or -client.EXTENSION suffix. The executable vault-pass receives no vault ID argument.
cards.misconception: Supplying a vault ID passes its label to any executable password-source script.

cards.statement: Ansible waits for a task to read a variable before decrypting a whole encrypted vars file.
cards.explanation: Ansible decrypts the whole encrypted file at load time, even if later tasks read just one variable from it.
cards.misconception: Ansible decrypts a whole variables file on demand for individual variable reads.

cards.statement: Ansible rejects a valid Vault password when its supplied vault ID label differs from the file's label.
cards.explanation: Vault ID labels are hints by default. A matching password decrypts content even when its supplied label differs.
cards.misconception: Ansible enforces matching vault ID labels with its default settings.

cards.statement: Passing several `--vault-id` options makes one ansible-playbook run read content encrypted with different passwords.
cards.explanation: Give one --vault-id label@source per password, for example dev@dev-password plus prod@prompt, and a single run can decrypt vaulted files and values made with each of them.

cards.statement: With DEFAULT_VAULT_ID_MATCH set, Ansible rejects a password that differs from one already used with the same vault ID.
cards.explanation: Ansible does not tie a vault ID label to one password, even with DEFAULT_VAULT_ID_MATCH enabled, so two files can carry the same label with different passwords.
cards.misconception: With DEFAULT_VAULT_ID_MATCH enabled, Ansible binds each vault ID label to a single password.

cards.statement: Ansible Vault stores an encrypted vault ID label beside the encrypted contents of a file.
cards.explanation: The vault ID label remains plain text in the header, making the label readable while the file's content stays encrypted.
cards.misconception: Vault encryption protects the vault ID label as part of the ciphertext.

cards.statement: `become_user: app` makes Ansible enable privilege escalation for that task.
cards.explanation: become_user selects the target account; enable escalation separately with become: true.
cards.misconception: Selecting become_user enables become.

cards.statement: With `become: true` and the target user omitted, Ansible runs the task as `root`.
cards.explanation: The default target account for privilege escalation on Linux is root.

cards.statement: With `become: true` and the method omitted, Ansible uses `sudo` for escalation.
cards.explanation: The escalation method selects the plugin that performs the account switch.

cards.statement: Ansible supports chaining `sudo` and `su` as the become methods for a single task.
cards.explanation: Choose one become method that reaches the target account directly.
cards.misconception: A become task can chain escalation methods.

cards.statement: A sudo rule for just `/bin/chmod` lets Ansible run `ansible.builtin.file` with `become: true` for an unprivileged login.
cards.explanation: Ansible invokes the module through a changing temporary file path, which a /bin/chmod-only rule does not authorize.
cards.misconception: Fixed-command permissions accommodate normal become tasks.

cards.statement: During delegation, `ansible_host` describes the original play host's connection address.
cards.explanation: A delegated task's ansible_host describes the delegated-to host.
cards.misconception: Delegation preserves the original host's connection address.

source.title: Controlling where tasks run: delegation and local actions

cards.statement: Ansible can delegate a task to a reachable IP address outside the inventory.
cards.explanation: An IP address or DNS name can identify a delegated host outside inventory.

source.title: Controlling where tasks run: delegation and local actions

cards.statement: A delegated host inherits the variables of the play host that delegates the task.
cards.explanation: Delegation copies none of the delegating host's host or group variables onto the delegated-to host, which keeps its own inventory variables.
cards.misconception: The delegated-to host inherits the delegating play host's variables.

source.title: Controlling where tasks run: delegation and local actions

cards.statement: With `delegate_facts: false`, Ansible assigns delegated facts to the delegated-to host.
cards.explanation: Delegated facts belong to the original play host unless delegate_facts is true.
cards.misconception: Fact ownership follows the execution destination.

source.title: Controlling where tasks run: delegation and local actions

cards.statement: `throttle: 1` on a delegated task that edits one shared file makes Ansible apply the edits one host at a time.
cards.explanation: Delegated tasks still run in parallel forks, so several play hosts can write one delegated file at once and overwrite each other. throttle: 1, serial: 1 or a run_once loop serializes the writes.

source.title: Controlling where tasks run: delegation and local actions

cards.statement: Ansible selects `ansible.builtin.linear` as the strategy for a play under the default configuration.
cards.explanation: Ansible's default strategy setting is linear, which applies when a play leaves its strategy unchanged.

cards.statement: With `strategy: free`, Ansible waits for a slow host to finish a task before advancing faster hosts.
cards.explanation: With the free strategy, a host that finishes a task advances while slower hosts remain on earlier tasks.
cards.misconception: The free strategy keeps hosts synchronized at task boundaries.

cards.statement: Ansible uses up to five parallel workers to execute tasks on target hosts with its default `forks` setting.
cards.explanation: forks caps concurrent workers used to execute tasks on target hosts; the default cap is five.

cards.statement: Ansible can use a percentage in a play's `serial` value to size host batches for a rolling update.
cards.explanation: Ansible calculates a percentage-based serial batch from the play's total host count.

source.title: Controlling playbook execution: strategies and more

cards.statement: A task's `throttle` value can raise Ansible's parallel worker count above its `forks` limit.
cards.explanation: throttle restricts task concurrency within existing forks and serial limits; it cannot raise those limits.
cards.misconception: throttle overrides the existing parallel-worker limit upward.

source.title: Controlling playbook execution: strategies and more

cards.statement: With `order: inventory`, Ansible guarantees the host sequence from the inventory source file.
cards.explanation: The inventory order comes from the compiled inventory selection; it may differ from the order of host definitions in a source file.
cards.misconception: Inventory order guarantees the sequence of host definitions in a source file.

source.title: Controlling playbook execution: strategies and more

cards.statement: With several serial batches, Ansible runs a `run_once: true` task once across the entire play's host set.
cards.explanation: run_once chooses one host in each serial batch, so a multi-batch play executes that task once per batch.
cards.misconception: run_once executes just once for the play regardless of serial batches.

source.title: Controlling playbook execution: strategies and more

cards.statement: With `async` and `poll: 0`, Ansible proceeds to the next task after starting the background job.
cards.explanation: The zero-poll setting leaves the job running while later tasks proceed; Ansible does not poll it for completion.

cards.statement: `tags: deploy` on `ansible.builtin.include_tasks` makes its loaded tasks inherit the `deploy` tag.
cards.explanation: Tags on include_tasks label the include itself. Use its apply option to add a tag to the tasks it loads.
cards.misconception: Tags assigned to a dynamic include flow to its loaded tasks.

cards.statement: Ansible selects a task with `tags: deploy` for a run that omits `--tags` and `--skip-tags`.
cards.explanation: Assigning a regular tag labels a task and leaves ordinary execution enabled. The run's --tags and --skip-tags options perform tag filtering.

cards.statement: Ansible assigns the `always` tag to its implicit fact-gathering task under the default configuration.
cards.explanation: The internal fact-gathering task carries the always tag in its default tag set.

cards.statement: `ansible-playbook --list-tags` lists tags defined inside files loaded by dynamic task includes.
cards.explanation: Tag previews exclude the contents of dynamic includes because those tasks are loaded during execution.
cards.misconception: Tag previews inspect the tasks inside dynamic includes.
